section.title: Make sure you want the life that comes with the goal
section.deck: Philip Su reflects on career ambition, early attainment, and the relationships that can be damaged along the way.

blocks.question: What advice would you give yourself at the beginning of your career?
answer: Su would first spend more time clarifying values and deciding what he actually wanted before committing to a direction. A clear target made earlier decisions easy—he could ask whether a job brought him closer to management—but he had not built an equally clear picture of what came after reaching that target.

He describes becoming a development manager and reaching a high level relatively young, then feeling that his purpose had disappeared. The “dog that caught the car” analogy captures a goal that gives direction until attainment exposes the missing plan for the rest of one’s life. He reports a difficult period of depression in that context. His advice is to consider the whole destination, not just its attractive feature, such as money or status.

He then recalls sleeping at the office and seeing his visiting fiancée only after work ended around 11 p.m. He says they remained together, but recognizes how easily the relationship could have broken under that treatment. Some things withstand strain and others do not recover. In hindsight, reaching his terminal level at 30 rather than 38 mattered less than he had assumed when compared with decades of work ahead and the health of his family relationships.

The question he would put to a highly ambitious younger person is therefore twofold: do you truly want the destination, and are you comfortable with what may break while pursuing it? This is his reflection on a particular period of his life, not a universal price that every ambitious career must pay.

followups.question: Would your younger self actually have accepted that advice?
answer: Su says no. He thinks advice about money and happiness often fails to land when the listener assumes they will be the exception. He was not mature enough then to receive the lesson. The value of a useful message therefore depends partly on readiness, not simply on whether the adviser can state it clearly.
